series.title: Annotation quality control and biological assays

lessons.title: Find spaCR on GitHub, PyPI and conda-forge
lessons.description: Find the official package and installer sources, compare the release available on each channel, and choose the matching installation tutorial.
objectives: Find the official download pages.
Choose the installation route for your computer.
Open the matching installation tutorial.
lessons.prerequisite: Open a web browser and decide whether you want a desktop installer or a Python environment.

scenes.narration: Choose how you want to install spaCR. Use a desktop installer for a ready-to-launch application, pip for a Python virtual environment, or conda-forge for a Conda environment. Start from the official spaCR links shown here.

On PyPI, find spaCR and read the installation command beside the current release. Copy that command when you are ready to install into your Python environment. The pip tutorial shows how to create and activate that environment first.
Use Project links to open the documentation, source repository or issue tracker. Bookmark the documentation so you can return to the module walkthroughs while working in spaCR.
On GitHub, open the spaCR repository. Main contains the release source, and nightly contains the latest development work. For a packaged desktop installation, open Releases and choose a release.
Expand Assets and download the installer for Windows, macOS or Linux. The Platform installers lesson explains installation, launching spaCR and uninstalling it on each operating system.
On conda-forge, open the spaCR package page and check the available version. Package channels can update at different times, so select the version available through the route you choose.

The conda-forge command installs spaCR into your active Conda environment. Follow Install spaCR to create that environment, install the package and launch the application. That lesson also explains package and environment removal.

Continue with Install spaCR for pip or conda-forge, or Platform installers for a desktop installer. Both lessons include uninstall guidance. Once spaCR opens, move to Home, then the pipeline overviews to choose a workflow for your data.

lessons.title: Install spaCR
lessons.description: Install with pip, conda-forge or Docker; check the installation, launch the appropriate interface, update and uninstall.
objectives: Choose an isolated Python installation or a versioned container.
Activate the correct environment before installing or launching.
Check the installed version, update and uninstall safely.
lessons.prerequisite: Use Python 3.12 for the virtual-environment route, or install Conda/Miniforge for either Conda route. Open a terminal. Existing environments need distinct names. For containers, install Docker Desktop or Docker Engine configured for Linux x86-64 containers.

scenes.narration: Choose one installation route. Pip installs spaCR inside a Python virtual environment or a Conda environment. Conda-forge installs into a Conda environment. Docker runs the command-line pipelines inside a container. Choose the route that fits how you will use spaCR.
For pip with a virtual environment, create a dedicated folder and run Python three point twelve with dash m venv to create dot venv. Use a different folder if it already contains an environment.

Activate dot venv before every install, update or launch. On Linux and macOS, source its bin slash activate script. In Windows PowerShell, run dot venv backslash Scripts backslash Activate dot ps one. The environment prompt and Python path confirm which interpreter you are using.

With the environment active, upgrade pip, then run pip install spacr. The package installation includes the Qt dependencies used by the desktop application. Wait for the scientific and desktop dependencies to finish installing.
Check the installed version and package path, then run python dash m pip check. Keep the version with your analysis notes.
Run spacr-doctor and follow any missing-dependency guidance relevant to your work. Then enter spacr to launch the installed application. Close the application before changing its environment.

For pip inside Conda, create an environment named spacr-pip with Python three point twelve and pip, then activate it. Conda supplies the interpreter; pip will supply spaCR. Choose a distinct name if spacr-pip already exists.

With spacr-pip active, upgrade pip and run pip install spacr. The package installation includes its Qt desktop dependencies. Check the package version and run pip check, just as in the virtual-environment route. Launch spacr from this same active environment.

For conda-forge, create a new environment named spacr-conda with Python three point twelve and spacr from the conda-forge channel in one command. Solving the interpreter and spaCR together avoids adding the package into an unrelated environment.
Conda shows its package plan before installing. Review it, accept the plan and let the downloads and installation finish.
Activate spacr-conda. Check the Python environment path and run conda list spacr to confirm the installed version and channel. Then run spacr-doctor and launch spacr from this environment.

For Docker, install Docker Desktop or Docker Engine using the official instructions for your operating system, and configure Linux containers. The spaCR images target x86 sixty-four. Use a container for command-line pipelines; choose a desktop installation for the graphical application.

Open the official spaCR container package page and select an available version. Pull that exact CPU image, then run it with spacr dash dash version and spacr-run dash dash list. Check that the reported version matches your selected tag. Keep that tag with your analysis notes.

Mount your project folder at slash data and your model cache at slash models. Export the pipeline settings into the project folder, and use container paths in the settings. Run spacr-run with the pipeline name and the settings CSV. Write results under slash data so they remain in your project after the container exits. On Linux, pass your user and group identifiers so output ownership matches your account.

For NVIDIA processing, install a supported host driver and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit, then configure the Docker runtime using its official guide. The CUDA twelve point four image needs host driver five hundred fifty or newer. Select the matching versioned CUDA image and add dash dash gpus all. The CPU image needs neither the toolkit nor a GPU.
Launch spaCR from the environment you installed. Home groups the modules into Core, Data, Tools and Organism. Choose a module to start its workflow.

To update a pip installation, close spaCR, activate its environment and run pip install dash dash upgrade spacr. Check the version afterwards. Use pip for spaCR updates in both pip routes, including the Conda environment created for pip.

For the conda-forge route, close spaCR, activate spacr-conda and run conda update dash c conda-forge spacr. If no newer build is available, Conda reports that the requested packages are already installed. Check the installed version rather than assuming the interface has changed.

To remove a pip installation, activate its environment and run python dash m pip uninstall spacr, then accept the removal prompt. This removes the spaCR package. It does not remove your microscopy projects or automatically remove every dependency.

If dot venv was created only for spaCR, deactivate it and remove that dedicated dot venv folder. For the dedicated spacr-pip Conda environment, run conda deactivate, then conda env remove dash n spacr-pip. Remove only the environment you created for this tutorial.

In the conda-forge environment, conda remove spacr removes the package after you review its removal plan. To remove the entire dedicated environment instead, deactivate it and run conda env remove dash n spacr-conda. Keep your project folders separately; uninstalling the environment is not deleting your analysis data.

lessons.title: Install spaCR with a desktop installer
lessons.description: Download the installer for your operating system, complete setup and open spaCR.
objectives: Download and run the installer for your operating system.
Choose an acceleration option and first-launch preferences.
Open spaCR and find installation logs if setup needs attention.
Uninstall the application using the operating-system or bundled removal route.
lessons.prerequisite: Download the official installer for your operating system and allow space for the application and its scientific dependencies.

scenes.narration: Open the official spaCR release on GitHub and, under Assets, download the installer for your operating system. These online installers download the Python runtime and scientific packages during setup.

On Windows, run the setup executable and follow its prompts. Leave automatic acceleration selected to use the supported hardware detected on your computer, or choose CPU-only operation if that is what you need.

On macOS, open the universal package and follow the installer. Start spaCR from its application launcher, and allow the first-run downloads to finish. Read any security prompt and confirm that the package came from the official release.

On Linux, make the downloaded installer executable, then run it from a terminal. Automatic acceleration selects a supported backend. The help lists dash dash torch-backend cpu for CPU-only operation, and dash dash skip-system-deps for computers that already have the Qt graphics libraries.
After setup, the installation profile records the selected backend. Check this when you want to confirm whether the runtime uses CPU or a supported accelerator.
Check the installed spaCR version. Keep it with your analysis notes, especially when you update the application later.
Setup asks about optional diagnostic sharing and account setup. Answer y only for the options you want; n, the default, keeps each one off. The Windows installer shows the same choices as checkboxes.

Open Preferences and choose Performance. Select a profile for your computer. Laptop uses fewer resources; higher profiles allow more caching and background work. Start with a modest profile if memory is limited.
Home groups the modules into Core, Data, Tools and Organism. Continue to Home screen and navigation to find the module for your next task.

Run spacr-doctor from the installed runtime if startup or a file format needs attention. Check the backend result and whether the GPU probe ran. If the warning identifies a missing optional CZI reader, install that extra only when you need CZI files.

For installation problems, find install dot log and install-profile dot json in the installation directory. Review the logs before sharing them with a support request. Include your operating system and spaCR version so the problem is easier to diagnose.

On Windows, close spaCR, open Settings, then Apps and Installed apps. Choose spaCR and Uninstall. The installed Uninstall executable is another route to the same removal process. Keep your project folders separately.

On macOS, close spaCR and run the bundled uninstall-spacr script in Library slash Application Support slash spaCR. It removes the application and its system launchers. The per-user runtime in your own Library slash Application Support slash spaCR is separate; remove it only if you also want to discard that runtime.

On Linux, close spaCR and run the uninstall-spacr script under your home folder, dot local slash share slash spacr. It removes the managed runtime and application launchers. Uninstallation does not require deleting your microscopy projects or their analysis results.

lessons.title: Home screen and navigation
lessons.description: Tour every current Home module from left to right, then learn the shared module controls using Mask and adjust navigation, help and appearance.
objectives: Identify every module in the current Core, Data, Tools and Organism rows.
Use Mask to recognize shared settings, previews, actions and outputs.
Return Home, use search and arrange panels.
Choose appearance and performance settings.
lessons.prerequisite: Install spaCR and open the desktop application.

scenes.narration: Home is the starting point. Read each row from left to right: Core, Data, Tools and Organism. Every tile opens its named module. The sidebar provides the same routes, and Home returns to this overview.
Mask generates object masks from microscopy images. We will open it briefly later to learn the controls shared by analysis modules.
Measure combines images and masks to extract object measurements and crops. Its measurement tables connect images to later analyses.
Annotate lets you inspect object crops and record reviewed labels for examples.
Classify trains a model on reviewed labels and scores other objects, using image crops or measured features.
Map Barcodes reads sequencing data to count and identify guides or barcodes.
Regression relates phenotype scores to sequencing guide counts, preserving the experimental grouping.
Import prepares incoming microscopy files and metadata for the project structure.
Embeddings encodes object crops into numerical features for exploration and comparison.
Run Compare brings saved run results together so you can inspect differences.
Experiment Design lays out conditions, wells and sample identities before an experiment.
Power / Design explores sample-size and power assumptions when planning comparisons.
Dose-Response fits responses across concentrations, keeping the chosen endpoint and controls explicit.
QC lists the saved quality reports of a project and marks the ones that are missing.
Make Masks lets you draw and review masks by hand, or prepare image-mask pairs.
Align & Stitch joins compatible image tiles and records their geometry.
Image UMAP projects object features so you can explore similar objects and inspect representative crops.
Gate Editor defines selections on real data columns. Review selected objects before turning a gate into labels.
Graph Builder creates plots from measurement tables with configurable columns and grouping.
The Organism row contains Toxoplasma. It opens an organism guide, an interactive diagram and the available Toxoplasma assay routes. The separate Toxoplasma tutorial explores this page.

Open Mask as a generic example of an analysis module. Here we are learning the screen layout, rather than completing a segmentation workflow. Settings sit on the left, the console and progress panels on the right, and actions along the bottom. Live opens the module’s preview when input data is available.

Settings are grouped into sections. Expand a section to see its controls. Choose your own input folder or use Load test data when a supplied example is available. Labels and help explain what each setting expects.

Import settings brings a saved configuration into this form. Run starts the chosen work and Stop asks a running job to stop. The console reports progress and messages. Check the module-specific tutorial before starting an analysis.

Drag the divider to give the settings or preview more space. Control plus the mouse wheel changes the text size in a column. These layout controls help you read the settings without changing the analysis itself.

Back on Home, the column on the right keeps track of your work. Recent runs lists what you ran, Totals counts runs, masks and measurements, and System shows the load on your computer. While a run is going or waiting, it appears here too. The Text size slider under the lowest panel makes this column's text larger or smaller.

The arrow handle on the column's left edge works like the module handles. Drag it to make the column wider or narrower, or click it to fold the column away so the tiles get the whole width. Click the arrow again to bring the column back.

Type a module, setting or function name into the search field beside Help. Here, searching for Performance finds the matching Preferences page. Click a result to open its destination. API results open the documentation for the selected function.

Press Control-K anywhere to open the command palette. Start typing a name, such as Measure, and the list narrows as you type. Press Enter to jump to the highlighted module, recent run or menu action without reaching for the mouse.

In Preferences, choose a Performance profile for your computer. Laptop uses fewer resources; the higher profiles allow more caching and background work. Start with a modest profile if memory is limited. Your analysis settings stay under your control in each module.

The General tab of Preferences sets the interface language, the font and GUI scale, whether the app dock stays open, and a palette for plots that suits colour vision deficiency. The Figures tab chooses the format and resolution of saved figures, and Appearance controls when tooltips appear.

Appearance decides how help appears as you work. Tooltip delay sets how long the pointer rests before a floating tip appears: two seconds by default, or zero for immediate tips. Show tooltips controls those floating tips. The dedicated help areas on Home and in Preferences show their text immediately. Theme and Animation fold open below to set the window's appearance.

Theme and Animation are folded sections of Appearance. Click Theme to open it: it sets the interface theme and page opacity, whether fields fade towards the right, and the window rim, with its length, how closely it follows the pointer, its alignment, mode and cycle. The Theme list also offers High contrast, which strengthens the contrast between text, controls and background.

Click Animation to choose the main backdrop and its palette. Animation colours sets the primary and accent colours for Custom colours; Animation background chooses an independent background, and Theme colour restores the page theme. Detail controls rendering resolution. Speed, Size and Density change motion and population. Mouse gravity radius sets mouse influence; zero disables it. Dot blinking controls white flashes. Field ripples sets the strength of ripples from clicks, opening or closing containers, popups and window snapping, independently of mouse gravity; zero turns ripples off, including the automatic popup waves. Click ripples decides whether a click on the background sends a ripple. Popup wave frequency sets how many waves per minute spread from an open popup window into spaCR field. Settings animation speed, Settings animation size, Settings animation detail and Settings animation density change only the Settings backdrop. Settings backdrop darkness controls the form’s readability.

Click Apply to preview your changes while Preferences stays open. A separate question asks whether to Keep or Revert the applied settings. Revert restores the previous settings; your edited controls remain available so you can adjust them or apply again.
Keep accepts the applied settings and leaves Preferences open. Continue adjusting another tab, or click Save when you are ready to keep the current values and close the window.

On the Modules tab, Session decides whether spaCR reopens the last module, settings and folder when it starts. Update channel chooses stable releases or nightly builds, and Proxy and Certificate bundle let downloads work behind an institutional proxy.

The Storage tab sets how long spaCR keeps its daily logs, run logs and run folders, and a size cap for each. Below them, the cache list shows where models and downloads are stored, with Clear and Move for each cache.
Prune now never deletes without asking. With a short example limit for run folders, it lists what it would delete in each folder and waits for an answer. Click Cancel and nothing is removed.

In Spaceout mode, Preferences includes spaCR field controls for eight independent effects. Turn each effect on or off separately. Ordinary appearance and settings-window animation controls remain available; Apply previews a change, Keep accepts it and Revert restores the previous choice.

lessons.title: Python API and batch commands
lessons.description: Find an analysis function, load saved settings, check the inputs and run spaCR from a terminal.
objectives: Find the installed batch commands and their Python functions.
Inspect a function signature and its API reference.
Check saved settings before running an analysis.
lessons.prerequisite: Install spaCR and activate its Python environment. Follow the Regression tutorial to prepare paired score/count tables and save the analysis settings. Use your own file paths in the commands.

scenes.narration: Activate the Python environment where you installed spaCR. Import spacr and print its version with the command shown. Keep the version with your analysis notes so you can reproduce the same run later.

Run spacr-run with dash dash list to find the available batch commands. The list shows each command key and its Python function. Choose the command for your task, such as mask, measure or regression. Use the desktop application for interactive tasks such as labelling images in Annotate.

Run spacr-run with dash dash describe followed by regression. Read the required inputs, defaults and function name. Here, the batch command calls perform_regression in spacr.ml. Open that function in the API reference to read its parameters and returned results.

In Python, import the function you need and inspect its signature. This example imports build_report from spacr.report. Look up the same name in the API reference, prepare the required arguments, and call the function from your script or notebook.

Save the settings from your module workflow, then pass the file with dash dash settings. Add dash dash dry-run to check the configuration and input paths. In this Regression example, the settings pair phenotype scores with guide counts for each plate. Read the messages and correct any missing inputs before continuing.

To execute the analysis, run the same command without dash dash dry-run. Follow the console until the command finishes, then inspect the outputs described by that module’s tutorial and API page. Keep the settings file, input tables, package version and console log with the results.

lessons.title: Mask: segment images and inspect the results
lessons.description: Load microscope images, choose segmentation settings, preview objects and save masks for measurement.
objectives: Load the microscopy example and identify its intensity channels.
Compare model settings and object-size filters in Live preview.
Run segmentation, inspect its figures and find the merged outputs.
lessons.prerequisite: Open Mask and choose Load test data. For your own images, prepare a source folder with consistent filenames and known channel identities. This example uses nucleus channel 0, cell channel 1 and pathogen channel 2, with an additional intensity channel 3.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Mask. Use this module to outline cells, nuclei and pathogens in microscope images. This walkthrough processes two-dimensional images. The Time, three-dimensional and OPS workflows have their own tutorials.

If your images are scattered across folders or named in a way Mask cannot read, click Organize images at the top of Input & Metadata. Give each channel a column, by dropping its folder or by a regex, and check that every row is one complete field. Apply moves the images into one folder with Yokogawa names and points Source at it, with the channels already filled in.

Click Load test data and wait for the microscopy example to load. Check Source before continuing. For your own images, select their folder and confirm that the filenames identify the plate, well, field and channel.

Check the channel assignments against the images. In this example, nucleus intensity is channel zero, cell intensity is channel one, and pathogen intensity is channel two. Channel three is an additional intensity image. Choose only the object types present in your experiment.

Below the inputs, the per-object table holds the settings you choose for each object. Each object is a column, here cell, nucleus and pathogen, and each row asks one question: whether to remove background, the object diameter, the segmentation model, the background level and the signal-to-noise cutoff. Add a filter adds a row that removes objects by a measured property such as area, and Add an organelle adds another object column.
Turn on Live and select a field. Inspect the image and proposed masks together before running the full folder. Try several fields that represent the range of image quality in your experiment.
Open Live settings and choose the model for the object you want to segment. Set the approximate object diameter, then click Run preview.
When the preview finishes, compare the outlines with the image. Look for missed objects and for neighbouring objects joined into one. The status line reports how many objects were found.

Use the minimum-area filter to hide objects smaller than the chosen number of pixels. Increasing it removes small labels from the preview. This filter updates an existing mask result, so you can compare size cutoffs quickly.

Set the minimum area back to zero to bring every object back. If the model splits or joins objects at the wrong scale, change Diameter and run the preview again, checking the boundaries as well as the count. Restore the settings you want before the batch run.

For a quick first run, use centred crops of two example fields as Source. With your own data, turn on Test mode and choose a few test images. Keep Plot on, check the per-object diameters and flow thresholds, keep Save on under Quality Control, then click Run.

When the run finishes, the figure list fills with its plots. The last figure draws each object's outlines on its own channel, nuclei, cells and pathogens, and the combined objects on the right. Check small objects, touching cells and missed regions in each figure.

The other figures show each channel and the mask and flow arrays the model produced. The run writes a merged folder with the image intensities and the final object labels, and keeps its plane-layout metadata beside the arrays so Measure can identify each channel and mask. Keep the inputs, settings, masks and quality reports together, then continue to Measure to extract object features and crops.

lessons.title: Measure: extract object features and crops
lessons.description: Load images with masks, inspect objects, choose crop settings and save measurements for annotation and classification.
objectives: Identify intensity channels and mask planes in the example.
Inspect fields and choose saved-crop normalization deliberately.
Run Measure and locate the database, object crops and figures.
lessons.prerequisite: Use the merged outputs from Mask, or choose Load test data in Measure. The example supplies sixteen fields with intensity planes 0–3 and cell, nucleus and pathogen masks in planes 4, 5 and 6.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Measure. Under Input and Experiment, use Source to select the merged folder containing your images and object masks, or click Load test data. Here the example is already loaded. Measure extracts features such as area and intensity, pairs related objects, and can save object crops for Annotate and Classify.

Click Load test data and wait for the example to load, or select your own merged project. Check the plane mapping: this example has four intensity channels followed by cell, nucleus and pathogen masks in planes four, five and six. When you press Run, Measure compares these mask planes with the layout stored for the folder; if they disagree, it offers Use stored image layout and asks you to review the mapping and run again.

To inspect these sixteen-bit example crops, turn Normalize on before opening Live. This makes the preview easier to see. Remember that this main setting also affects saved crops; we will switch it off before this batch run.
Turn on Live and choose a field. Inspect the object crops and their mask relationships. Scroll through the categories and enlarge the preview if needed to see the boundaries clearly.

Use the displayed-channel selector to inspect one intensity channel at a time. Channel zero shows a grayscale view; All channels restores the combined view. This selector changes the preview without changing the labels or batch channel mapping.
Choose another field and compare its objects. If masks are missing or joined incorrectly, correct them or adjust Mask before continuing.

To compare fields side by side, open Checked images and tick the fields you want. The grid groups the crops by their source field; hover a crop to see its path, or double-click it to open that exact field. Uncheck all images clears the grid. This changes only the preview, not what Measure processes.

To check segmentation quality across the project before measuring, turn on QC in the Actions row, beside 3D and Time. Its popup lists the fields and wells whose masks look unusual, such as far fewer objects than the rest of the plate, with links to inspect them. The check is advisory and never stops Measure; closing the popup turns the switch off.

Under All settings, Image Preprocessing holds the corrections Measure can apply to each field before measuring: Image Deconvolution with a point spread function, and Illumination Correction with a model you estimated earlier. They change the pixels that are measured in this run; the masks and the arrays on disk are not changed.

Turn Live off and restore Normalize off for this example. Choose normalization deliberately when saving crops: per-crop scaling changes the intensity differences visible to a later image classifier. Keep the original merged arrays for quantitative measurements.

Once the settings look right, keep them. Open Templates on the settings strip, or press Ctrl+Shift+R, and choose Save current settings. Give the template a name you would say out loud; next time you apply it instead of retyping.
Import also reads the settings CSV that every run writes next to its results. An earlier run's configuration, or a colleague's, becomes a template named after the file.
Rename gives an imported template a clearer name. Share writes the selected one to a file for others, and Apply loads it into Measure.

Keys such as Ctrl+Shift+R can be changed. Open Help, then Keyboard shortcuts, and choose Change shortcuts. Type a new key for any action; if it clashes with another, spaCR names the conflict and keeps Save off until you resolve it.

Enable saving measurements and object crops, keep Plot on, and choose the crop size and output channels. For a first run, Test mode measures one field; turn it off to process all sixteen supplied fields. Click Run and follow the console until the run completes, then check which fields succeeded before proceeding.

Inspect the crop figure, then locate measurements.db in the measurements folder and the saved object images in the project’s crop output. Keep the database and image paths together. Continue to Annotate to label example objects, or to Classify when you already have labelled training data.

Before any run starts, spaCR estimates the memory each worker needs from one field of your project. With very large fields, such as stitched mosaics, the workers you asked for may not fit in the free RAM, and spaCR asks first. Choose the recommended worker count, keep yours and let Measure pause new fields while memory is short, or close other programs to free memory.

lessons.title: Annotate: label objects and save your annotations
lessons.description: Load example crops, choose an annotation column, label objects, adjust the view and prepare your labels for classification.
objectives: Load saved crops or stream crops from merged images.
Choose an annotation column, assign and clear labels, and save your changes.
Adjust channel colours and review class counts and coverage.
Find Agreement and the image and feature training routes.
lessons.prerequisite: Open Annotate from Home. Use Load test data and choose Load for the example crops and measurements database. For your own project, use the folder containing its measurements database and crops or merged images.

scenes.narration: Open Annotate from Home. The grid shows individual objects from your project. You will label these objects and save the labels in the measurements database.
Click Load test data and choose Load. This downloads the example image crops and their measurements database, then opens them in Annotate.
Choose Stream when you want to read crops directly from merged images. Choose Load for already exported crops. We will use Load for this walkthrough.
To open your own data, click Open source and select the plate folder containing measurements and the image data. The grid then loads the objects from that project.
Inspect the crop grid. Use the page controls to browse the objects. Adjust the crop size if you need a closer view or want more objects on each page.
Open Settings and choose an annotation column. Create a new column to keep this labelling task separate from existing annotations. Decide what each class represents before you start.
Left-click a crop to assign class one. Right-click assigns class two. Click the same class again to clear it. The coloured ring shows the label, and the white ring marks the focused crop.
Press Next to move to the next page and submit your labels for saving. Wait for saving to finish before closing the application.

Press Back to return to the previous page and check your labels. You can also use keys one to nine to assign classes and zero to clear a label. The on-screen legend lists the navigation and undo shortcuts.
Open Class counts to see how many objects you have labelled in each class. Use this to find classes that need more examples.
Open Coverage to see how your annotations are distributed across the project. Include examples from the conditions and image groups you want the classifier to recognize.
To clear a label, click the same class again. Move to the next page to save the change, then return to check the cleared crop.
In Settings, Channel colours selects the display palette. Display order assigns source channels to the colour slots. Choose a view that makes your classes easy to distinguish.
Here is the CMY palette. You can return to RGB through the same settings. Keep the view consistent while comparing and labelling objects.
Open Annotator Agreement from the icon at the top right to compare annotation columns. Use it to find objects where reviewers assigned different labels.
When your labels are ready, open Train. Choose images for an image classifier or measured features for a tabular classifier. The linked Classify lessons explain the training settings.

Suggest proposes labels for the crops you have not answered yet, so first give it examples of both classes from several wells. Here a few crops of each class are labelled in three wells, then Next saves them.

Open Suggest and choose Suggest for the images on this page. The round takes a few seconds, and the unlabelled crops on the page now wear question-mark badges. The bar above the grid counts how many suggestions are left to judge.

Click a suggested crop or press Y to confirm it, and right-click it or press N to reject it. Both answers remain pending until Next saves them; rejections train the next round, and Confirm the rest of the page settles what is left once you have checked it.
Generate annotation database creates a crop set from suitable source data. Use it when preparing a new annotation project; the downloaded example already includes the crops and database needed here.
Open Console to check source-loading and save messages. Your annotation column is stored in the project database and can be selected when you prepare training data in Classify.
For help with a setting, open spaCR AI in Console after configuring a provider in Preferences. When you have finished labelling, continue to Classify with your project and chosen annotation column.

lessons.title: Classify: train an image classifier
lessons.description: Prepare labelled image crops, choose the computer-vision family, train a small model and find its predictions.
objectives: Prepare the downloadable image-classification example.
Choose the model, image channels and training settings.
Keep wells separate and inspect saved models and predictions.
lessons.prerequisite: Download the measured example through Annotate using Load test data, then Load. Keep its plate1 folder with measurements/measurements.db and the png crops. Download Classify_existing_split_example.zip below and extract the helper. In your spaCR environment, run prepare_classify_split.py --source /path/to/plate1 --destination /path/to/new_split. Select the new_split folder in Classify. The helper is for this four-well example; it copies 64 labelled RGB crops into train and test folders.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Classify and choose Computer Vision, Torch. This family learns from labelled object crops and saves a model that can score other crops. Follow the Annotate lesson first to download the example images and their labels.

In Annotate, choose Load test data, then Load. Keep the plate folder containing measurements and PNG crops. For your own data, start with crops from Measure and assign the classes you want to learn in Annotate.

Download the linked example ZIP and extract prepare_classify_split.py. Run it in your spaCR environment with source pointing to the example plate folder and destination pointing to a new folder. The helper prepares sixty-four labelled images for this exercise.

Open the new folder and its manifest. The train and test directories each contain two class folders. The manifest lists each copied image and its well. Keep whole wells on one side of the split when images from the same well share experimental conditions.

Return to Classify and choose the prepared folder as Source. Select the parent containing train and test. Keep that prepared folder for the rest of this lesson so the model and its output files stay together.

Turn Generate training dataset off because the helper has already prepared the split. Enable Train and Test. Leave application to the full dataset off for this first run. The model uses class indices zero and one for the two class folders.

Choose ResNet18, image size one hundred twenty-eight, all three RGB channels, batch size eight and one epoch. Set loader workers to two, with pretrained weights and augmentation off for this short example. Epochs controls how many times training passes through its input images.

Set validation fraction to one half, keep grouping by well and leave the leakage checks enabled. Validation monitors the model during training; the separate test folder is used for the final assessment. Check the reported well assignments before interpreting the scores.

Turn Plot on, clear the settings search and press Run. Watch the console for dataset loading, the resolved split, training progress and output paths. Wait for training and testing to finish before opening the saved results.

Open Figures to inspect loss and accuracy. One epoch gives a quick first pass. Compare the test results across classes before increasing training time. If predictions favour only one class, review the labels, class balance and input channels before using the model on a larger dataset.

Open model, resnet18, rgb, epochs underscore one inside the prepared folder. Keep the checkpoint, model card and result tables together. Use the saved predictions to review errors, then continue to Classifier Evaluation or Activation Maps to inspect the model further.

lessons.title: Classify: learn from measured features
lessons.description: Load measurements, define classes, train a tabular classifier and inspect object scores and plate summaries.
objectives: Select the tabular family and a measured project.
Define classes and choose feature channels, model size and held-out wells.
Find model outputs, object predictions and summary figures.
lessons.prerequisite: Use Load test data in Classify and choose Load, then confirm the downloaded plate folder with Choose source data. For your own project, run Measure first. The example uses columnID values c1 and c2 as two classes; use labels appropriate to your experiment when working with your own data.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Classify and choose Tabular Machine Learning. This family uses the object measurements saved by Measure. It produces a fitted model and a score for each object with the required measurements.
Click Load test data and choose Load. Wait for the measured example to download. For your own data, select the project folder created by Measure, including its measurements database.

Use Choose source data to confirm the downloaded plate folder. Select the folder containing measurements. This gives the classifier access to the object tables and the metadata used to define classes.

Choose metadata as the class basis and define two Classes using column I D values c1 and c2. These labels distinguish the two plate columns in the example. To train from your own cell annotations, choose the annotation basis and the label column you created in Annotate.

Set Channel of interest to one for the example. This controls which channel-specific measurement features enter the model. For your own experiment, select the channel that contains the signal relevant to your classes.

Choose Random Forest, sixteen estimators and two worker jobs. Estimators controls the number of trees. More trees increase fitting work. Leave feature pruning and cross-validation off for this first pass; you can compare those choices after you have a working baseline.

Set Test size to one tenth and keep grouping by well. spaCR holds out complete wells, so the final fraction of objects can differ from the requested fraction. Read the resolved split in the console and make sure it suits your experiment.

Enable Plot, clear the search and press Run. The console shows feature filtering, the training and test split, model fitting and the saved output paths. Wait for the run to finish before comparing its scores.

Find the results under results, random_forest, channel underscore one. The database stores the predicted class in predictions and the class-one probability in ml_pred. Objects missing required measurements can remain unscored; inspect missing values when exporting a summary.

Browse the feature-importance figures and plate heatmap. With Predictions and mean grouping, a well value is the average of its binary predicted classes. Use the saved object scores for detailed review, and compare held-out performance before applying the classifier to another experiment.

lessons.title: Map Barcodes: from sequencing reads to counts
lessons.description: Load paired reads and library references, find barcode positions, apply the settings and save guide counts.
objectives: Download a small paired-read example and select matching reference tables.
Inspect barcode positions and orientation before applying a proposal.
Run mapping and inspect count and quality-control outputs.
lessons.prerequisite: Choose Load test data in Map Barcodes. The example uses SRR33531217 reads, the matching primers_3 column and row tables, and guide references. Use reference tables matching your own library when processing other reads.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Map Barcodes. The inputs are sequencing reads and reference tables that name the barcodes in your library. The output counts each observed combination, ready for sequencing quality control and downstream analysis.
Click Load test data and select both mates of the first archive run. Limit each file to ten thousand reads for this example, then wait for the paired sample to download.

Select the matching column, row and guide reference tables. Each table pairs barcode names with sequences. Keep those names consistent with the plate layout and guide identifiers used by the rest of your analysis.
Open Find barcodes and start the search. The preview samples both mates and checks barcode positions and orientations. Wait for the results before changing the main form.

Compare Observed with By chance, then inspect the proposed orientation, offset and verdict for each barcode. Prefer positions supported by many reads and distinct expected references. Open the verdict explanation if the result is uncertain.

Inspect the guide results for both mates. In this example, read one supports the reverse-complemented guide sequence and read two supports the stored orientation. Use the results for your library and read pair when choosing an orientation.

Check the row barcode as well. Here, read one supports its reverse complement and read two supports the stored sequence. Review column, guide and row together so the complete combination identifies the intended well and guide.

Open the read viewer to inspect individual reads. Use the colour legend to find the column, guide, row and anchor segments. Check that the proposed positions agree with the expected library structure.

Review the proposed extraction settings, then click Apply these settings to copy them into the form. The example uses an extraction window of eighty-nine bases. Check the updated fields before starting the run.

Follow the orientation notes when selecting your final reference files. For this example, select reverse-complemented copies of the row and guide references and keep the column reference as stored. Preserve every barcode name when preparing those copies.

Choose the downloaded read pair, two workers and chunks of one thousand reads. Enable annotated-read saving if you want to inspect individual assignments. Click Run; this mapping workflow uses the CPU.

When mapping finishes, inspect unique_combinations.csv and the quality-control outputs. The count table links column, row and guide names with read counts. Review unmatched and ambiguous assignments in Barcode QC, then pair these counts with phenotype scores in Regression.

lessons.title: Regression: from paired tables to results
lessons.description: Pair phenotype scores with guide counts, choose an inference method, run the example and explore guide and gene results.
objectives: Load paired score/count tables and choose an output folder.
Set the inference method, reporting level and analysis unit.
Run the example and inspect results with the accompanying diagnostics.
lessons.prerequisite: Open Regression and choose Load test data to obtain four paired score/count tables. Use a new output folder. A measurement database is optional for this score-and-count analysis; object-level views require the corresponding measured data and images.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Regression. This module relates phenotype scores to guide abundance. Start with a score table and a count table for each plate, then choose how to test and report associations.
In Input Tables, click Load test data and wait for the example to load. It provides four score tables and four count tables, paired by plate.
Inspect each paired row and check the plate name, score file and count file. Leave the optional measurement-database column empty for this example. Choose a new output folder for the analysis.

Switch to All settings and use the search box to find Inference. Choose nonparametric for this guide-permutation example. Use a parametric method when your question and design call for fitting predictors together.
Level chooses which results to report. Select both to obtain guide-level and gene-level results. Keep these testing families separate when reviewing adjusted significance.

Choose well as the analysis unit for this example. Review the response column, transformations, controls and excluded wells. Adapt these settings to the design of your own screen before running new data.
Minimum guide support controls how many wells must contain a guide before it is tested. Set it to two to follow this small example. Choose an appropriate support requirement for your experiment.

Set one hundred and ninety-nine permutations for a quick first run. More permutations give finer empirical p-value resolution and take longer. Choose a larger count when your final analysis requires it.

Set the permutation seed to zero to repeat the same randomization. Keep the example’s plate blocks and row and column nuisance terms. For your own data, choose blocks that respect which observations can be exchanged under the experimental design.
Choose none for Annotation source to run the example without gene-annotation lookup. For another screen, select annotations that match its organism and identifier system.

Clear the search, check the paired inputs and output folder, then click Run. Follow the console as the module aligns the tables, filters guides and calculates the results. Diagnostic figures are generated with the analysis.

When the run finishes, open Runs and select the saved analysis. Confirm the folder and settings before comparing it with another run. Rerun the analysis after changing settings if you want new results.

Open Results and use Level to switch between guide and gene results. Inspect the result table and interactive views. The saved results_grna.csv and results_gene.csv files contain the corresponding tables for further analysis.

Open the p-values view and the Diagnostics tool. Review the result distribution together with the permutation resolution, testing family and design warnings. Resolve important diagnostic concerns before interpreting associations.

Use the toolbar to open Volcano Explorer, Hit List or Investigate Hit for the next step. Their tutorials show how to inspect selected results. Keep the input tables, saved settings, result files and diagnostic reports together when sharing the analysis.

lessons.title: Make Masks: edit labels and prepare training images
lessons.description: Open image-mask pairs, correct objects, record verdicts, organize images and masks for Measure and create paired training crops. Draw, edit and export separate class-labelled YOLO boxes without changing the image or segmentation mask.
objectives: Open images with matching instance masks and inspect objects in the magnifier.
Correct labels with Undo, drawing, division, merging and object filters.
Save curated masks, record Keep or Discard verdicts and create image-mask crops for training.
Organize images and masks for Measure, and share curated pairs with Upload data.
Draw and edit separate class-labelled boxes, save their project and export normalized YOLO labels.
lessons.prerequisite: Prepare a folder of two-dimensional images with matching instance-label TIFFs in a masks subfolder. Each mask uses the image filename stem. Work on a copy when practising edits and recropping. The example uses ER images and cell masks from Measure’s downloadable microscopy project.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Make Masks in Tools. The buttons along the bottom left bring images in: Open folder, Organize for Measure and Load test data. On the right, Discard, Keep, Skip and Upload data decide what happens to each field once it is edited. Clear all objects, immediately left of Discard, asks for confirmation before removing every object in the current image.

Load test data opens ten example Toxoplasma images. Its arrow also offers a sample of each training dataset a published model learned from, with its masks, so you can see what good training pairs look like.

Click Open folder and select the image folder. For this example, use the ER intensity images and corresponding cell masks from the Measure sample. Keep the image and mask dimensions equal and their filenames paired.

The editor loads the image and its matching mask from the masks subfolder. Coloured labels identify individual objects. Check that the outlines follow the image boundaries. If a companion mask is missing, start with an empty mask and draw the objects you need.

Open the Live magnifier settings and keep Segment on Region under the mouse. The method comes from the Detection method category, here Otsu, which runs on the CPU. Choose a model-based method when thresholding does not separate your objects well.

Turn on Magnifier and hover over an object to preview its outline. The readout at the top left gives the pixel position and intensity, and the label and area of the object under the cursor. Click to add outlined objects when they look correct, or switch Magnifier off to continue editing.

Choose the tool that matches the correction. Brush adds pixels, Erase removes pixels and Erase object removes a whole label. Wand adds an intensity region by default; hold Ctrl and click to remove that region. Draw adds an outlined object; Divide / Merge splits with a left drag or joins objects with a right drag. Zoom helps you inspect boundaries before making changes.

Choose Erase object and click inside the object you want to remove. Check the updated outline and object count. Use this for an unwanted label, such as debris or an object outside your analysis criteria.
Click Undo to restore the deletion. Redo applies it again. Use these history controls to compare an edit with the previous mask, then return to the version you want to keep.

Select Draw and trace a closed boundary around a missing object. The editor fills it with a new label. In this practice step the outline is in the background, so undo it before saving. For training data, trace the actual object boundary.

Select Wand and click to add a connected intensity region. Set the tolerance and maximum pixels in Magic wand settings to control its extent. This background example demonstrates the gesture; use real object boundaries when preparing training masks.

Keep Wand selected, hold Ctrl and click to remove the intensity region. Release Ctrl to add again with the same button. Undo restores the previous edit. Here both practice clicks are undone before saving the original mask.

Use Divide when two touching objects share one label. Draw a cut across the whole joined region and inspect the separated labels. Undo the split if it cuts through one object or leaves an incorrect boundary.

Keep Divide / Merge selected and right-drag a line across the objects to join. They share the first crossed object’s label without filling the background between them. Undo restores the separate labels. Saved groups retain their shared label when you reopen the image.

Adjust Display percentiles to make dim structures easier to inspect. These controls change the image view while preserving raw intensity values and labels. Return to a consistent display when comparing fields.

To remove objects by size or shape, choose a property in the Filter category and click Add a filter. Any regionprop that scikit-image measures can be a filter, such as area, solidity or mean intensity. Here an area row with a minimum hides the smaller cells; press Filter to apply the list again. The ledger below names every object the filters hid.

Remove a row to bring back the objects it hid. The filters apply as you edit them and again whenever a field opens, so remove the rows you no longer want before moving on. Undo also reverses a filter step.
After reviewing the edits, click Save mask in the toolbar. Keep the source images together with the saved masks and their curation record.

Choose Box beside Draw to annotate separate YOLO bounding boxes. These boxes have their own classes and history; they do not replace the segmentation mask or change the acquired image. Here the boxes demonstrate interaction, not biological training truth.

Click Add class and enter a class name. This example uses demonstration. Select the intended class before drawing; keep class names and their numeric identifiers consistent across your training dataset.

Drag across the image to draw a box. The outline and class label show the new annotation. For real training data, enclose the target object accurately; this practice rectangle is only a gesture example.
Drag inside an existing box to move it. The box keeps its class while its image coordinates change. Inspect its position before saving.
Drag a corner of the box to resize it. Place the edges around the intended object and check that the rectangle remains inside the image.
Hold Control while dragging to draw another box inside an existing one. This creates a separate annotation rather than moving the outer box. Both boxes keep their own coordinates and class.
Right-click a box to delete it. Check which outline disappears, especially when boxes overlap. Removing a box does not erase pixels from the segmentation mask.
Click Undo to restore the deleted box. The two independent annotations return. Use history to recover a mistaken edit before saving.
Redo applies the deletion again. Undo once more to keep both demonstration boxes for the export. Review the final annotations before writing them to disk.

Click Save boxes to store the annotations in the project file beside the images. This saves box coordinates and classes separately from the mask. Keep the project file with its corresponding source images.

Click Export YOLO labels and choose the text-file destination. Each row contains a class identifier and normalized center X, center Y, width and height relative to the full image. The class-name companion preserves the identifier mapping.

A field with no annotated boxes exports an empty label file. This second microscopy field illustrates that file format, not a biological negative. Use negative training examples only after checking that no target objects are present.

Return to the first image. The saved boxes reload with the same classes and coordinates, while the acquired image and segmentation mask remain unchanged. Keep the YOLO labels, class mapping and source images together for training.

The icons at the top right open the rest of the mask toolkit. Cellpose Workbench trains a model on curated pairs and applies it to a folder, and the next icon runs detection on every field of the open folder.
Model Compare puts two sets of masks side by side and Model Zoo finds and tests weights. When more examples need fixing, Curate and Napari Bridge take you back into editing.

Choose Recrop and drag a box around the objects you want in a smaller training field. This writes a new image and matching mask. Objects cut by the boundary are dropped, so leave space around complete objects and inspect the crop.

Click Next image in the toolbar to open the new crop. The parent image and mask are retained in recropped_originals for recovery. Review the crop and its labels before adding it to your training dataset.
Image enhancement ends with Deep image enhancement. It restores the selected channel with a Cellpose 3 model in its own environment; the image on disk is never changed.
Choose Denoise, Deblur or One-click restoration, then open Restoration model settings. Pick weights for cells or nuclei and set the typical object diameter in pixels.
Load the model. On the CPU a whole field takes tens of seconds; the original intensities are kept for measurements.
Compare raw and enhanced shows both pictures side by side. The restored picture is model output, not new structure: check it before trusting masks drawn on it.
Apply uses the restored picture for display and detection only. Measurements still read the original pixels.

To detect objects with a model, choose Cellpose in the Detection method category and review its settings. This example uses cpsam, normalization on, cell-probability threshold zero and flow threshold zero point four. Check whether detections will replace existing labels or be added to them.

Click Object detection. The model runs in the background, and the result replaces the labels when it arrives. Compare the new outlines with the image, and undo a result that does not follow the object boundaries before adjusting the settings.

Open Cell probability to inspect the foreground score map. Use it to see which regions the model supports. Change the foreground threshold when useful, then run detection again to produce a new result.

Open Flows to inspect the directional view. The flow-consistency threshold controls which detected objects are retained: lower values are stricter, and zero disables this check. Compare the final masks after each setting change.
Undo restores the labels from before the detection. Keep the mask that best follows the image, and inspect each field's result before including it in training.

To detect faint puncta inside cysts, open the original single-channel image and keep the cyst instance masks in a separate folder with matching filenames. These punctum masks represent centre pixels, not complete object boundaries.

Choose Centre-pixel puncta within parent masks. Set the primary class to cyst and the secondary class to punctum, choose the parent-mask folder and press Reload. Review spot scales, the noise threshold, centre pixels, corrected intensity, peak spacing and edge margin.

Choose replace in Object operations, then click Object detection to process the whole image. This field yields 150 candidates and 46 included puncta. Detection uses original intensities; display normalization and enhancement do not alter this mode.

Save mask writes the label TIFF and a puncta CSV beside it. center20 is the mean of twenty centre pixels; local_bg records local background and center_corrected subtracts it from the configured centre mean. Inspect included and mask_pixels: shared pixels have one label owner, so a mask can contain fewer pixels. Original images and parent masks remain unchanged.

While you work through a folder, Keep and Discard record a verdict for each field and move on to the next. Nothing is deleted: the verdict goes to keep_discard.csv in the folder's csv subfolder, with the image, its mask and its current object count.

Discard marks a field you do not want in a training set. Skip belongs to curation sessions started from the terminal with spacr-make-masks: it marks a field that cannot be curated, so the next session does not offer it again.

When your curated pairs could help others, click Upload data. Choose the field on screen, every curated image with its saved mask, or an images folder and a masks folder, then name the dataset. The link shows the Hugging Face dataset it will join. Nothing is sent until you press Upload and agree to share.

Microscopes often save images in nested folders. When you open a folder whose images sit in subfolders, Make Masks offers to copy them into one new folder, each named after the folders it was in. The originals are not touched, and No opens the folder as it is.
The copies open in the editor, and a rename manifest records where each one came from. A field without a mask starts with an empty mask, ready for drawing or detection.

To measure your fields, click Organize for Measure. Measure reads each field as one merged array that holds every channel and its masks. Give a source folder here, or drop files and folders into the table below. If Consolidate subfolders is on and a copy fails, the popup says how many files failed and where the manifest is, and stops without changing the source or the table.

Drop each channel folder into the table: every folder becomes a column, and every row is one field. Add a mask column, set its role, here the cell masks of channel two, and drop the masks folder onto it. Files are matched across the columns by name.
Detect sets matches the images by name, order and size, then shows three example sets. Confirm them only when every set really belongs together; otherwise fix the regex or the columns first.

Set Show to Image plus text and Thumbnail quality to High to check the rows by eye; the quality changes only the display, never the masks or measurements. A cell that nothing matched stays empty and is flagged, and Apply waits until every row is complete.

Click Apply. The summary says what will happen: images and masks move into Yokogawa-named channel folders and are merged into merged. Files are moved, not copied, and every move is written to a manifest.

When sorting finishes, Make Masks opens the first channel folder, and the console notes that the result is first in Measure's recent sources. Open Measure and use it as the source to extract object features.

Keep curated images and their same-stem masks together. Use Cellpose Workbench to train on those pairs, or Organize for Measure and then Measure to extract measurements. The related tutorials show each next step.

lessons.title: Image UMAP: explore measurements with image crops
lessons.description: Select measurement tables, build a UMAP embedding and click points to inspect the corresponding objects.
objectives: Load a measured project and choose its feature tables.
Control neighbourhood size, point spacing and the sampled row count.
Run the embedding, inspect crops and find saved results.
lessons.prerequisite: Follow Annotate and choose Load test data, then Load, to obtain the measured example and its image crops. Keep the downloaded plate folder. For your own data, complete Measure with saved crops before opening Image UMAP.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Image UMAP. Use it to explore similarities between measured objects while viewing their image crops. Start with a project containing a measurements database and the crops saved by Measure.

Under Source, choose Add project folders and select the example plate folder downloaded through Annotate. Review the available databases, rows and shared columns. You can add more project folders when you want to compare several datasets.

Choose the tables whose features you want to compare. For this example, select cell, cytoplasm, nucleus and pathogen measurements. Leave Resnet features off to use the existing measurements. Review missing-data and correlated-feature settings before running.
Set Row limit to four hundred for a quick first view and use two workers. Row limit controls how many objects enter the embedding. Increase it when you are ready to explore more of the dataset.

Choose UMAP as the reduction method. Each point will represent an object using two plotted coordinates. You can explore PCA through its linked tool when you want a linear projection and feature loadings.

Set Neighbours to fifteen and Minimum distance to zero point one. Neighbours controls the size of the neighbourhood used to build the map. Minimum distance controls how closely points can pack in the displayed embedding.
Set Random seed to forty-two so repeated runs with the same inputs and settings are easier to compare. Save your chosen feature tables and preprocessing settings alongside the seed.
Clustering assigns labels to groups after the embedding is built. This example uses DBSCAN with noise removal off. Inspect the crops within any group before using its label in a later analysis.
Enable Plot images and Plot points. Use twelve small crop images so the overview remains readable. You can inspect individual objects more closely in the interactive view after fitting.
Press Run and watch the console for feature preparation and embedding progress. Wait for the completed result. If you change the input tables or reduction settings, run again to produce a new map.

Inspect the embedding in Figures and open the results folder reported in the console. Keep the saved figure, selected measurement rows, metadata and cluster labels together so you can trace an interesting group back to its objects.
Enable Interactive to explore the fitted map. Zoom into a region and click its points. The view uses the completed embedding, so you can inspect different objects without fitting it again.

Click a point to show its crop in the side panel. Use the displayed object path to connect the image to its source record. Compare morphology across nearby points and across distant regions of the map.

Click another point to compare its crop. The sidebar also provides selection labelling and cluster-label propagation. Those controls save annotations, so choose the intended label and selection before applying them.

Open Image Scatter from the Image UMAP header to compare selected features directly, or open PCA for a linear projection. Continue with the linked tutorials for their input settings and saved outputs.

lessons.title: Activation Maps: inspect an image classifier’s saliency maps
lessons.description: Select a trained classifier and matching image crops, compare channel and image saliency, and open the saved maps.
objectives: Match the crop archive, model and preprocessing settings.
Run channel saliency with an image overlay.
Compare image saliency and locate the saved grids.
lessons.prerequisite: Use a trained image-classification checkpoint and a TAR archive of compatible image crops. Retain the crop-format marker when present and follow the model card’s channel order, image size and normalization. The example uses four RGB crops from Annotate and a ResNet18 model from Classify. Train or obtain a model whose preprocessing is known before starting.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Classify, then Activation Maps. This tool shows where a trained image classifier’s prediction is sensitive to the input pixels. Start with the model and an archive of crops prepared in the same way as its training data.

Select the crop archive in Dataset. This example contains four RGB cell crops from Annotate. Include the crop-format marker when packaging the images, and keep their filenames so you can connect each map to its original object.
Select the trained model and choose its model type. Here the model is ResNet eighteen. Read its model card and set Image size to one hundred and twenty-eight to match the training input.
Set Channels to the order expected by the model. In this example the selector uses one, two and three for the RGB input. Preserve that order when comparing maps from different images.
Set Normalize input to match training. The separate display normalization controls how the image appears in the saved overlay. Keep both settings consistent when comparing runs.
Choose saliency channel and enable Overlay, Plot and Save. This produces separate channel maps over the images. For the four-crop example, use a batch size of four and one worker, then click Run.
Follow the console until processing finishes. If the Figures panel is empty, open the output folder and inspect the saved batch grids. Check error messages and the saved results before continuing.

Open batch_0_grid.png from the method’s batch_grids folder. Match each occupied slot with its source crop; unused slots may be blank. The corner labels are model predictions. Compare salient regions with the original image and known object boundaries.
To compare a combined map, select saliency image and turn Overlay off. Run the same images again with the same preprocessing. Keep the two methods’ outputs in their respective folders.

Open the second saved grid. Image saliency combines the channel sensitivities into one map for each crop. Compare the highlighted regions with the channel maps. The displayed colours indicate the map scale; interpreting them requires checking the model and image context.

Leave Correlation off for this first walkthrough. Review examples from different classes, including prediction errors, before interpreting patterns. Use Classifier Evaluation to assess performance on independently held-out data.

Keep the input archive, model and model card, settings, maps and output database together. Return to the original crops to investigate unexpected regions, or compare another method using the same inputs.

lessons.title: Timelapse
lessons.description: Link objects across a time series, inspect their tracks, and prepare the tracked images for measurement.
objectives: Load the example images and masks in Track preview.
Adjust overlap and inspect object identities across frames.
Configure a time-series Mask run and find its tracked outputs.
lessons.prerequisite: Download and extract SYNTHETIC_timelapse_preview.zip. The teaching example contains eight cell-image frames and matching label images. For a full Mask run on your own data, prepare time-ordered microscopy images and record the acquisition interval.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Mask, turn on Time in the Actions row and switch on Timelapse to turn tracking on. Timelapse links objects across consecutive images. We will first try the linked example in Track preview, then review the settings for processing your own image sequence.

Download and extract the example archive below, then click Track preview at the right of the Actions heading. The archive contains an image sequence and a matching mask sequence for eight frames. Keep both folders together so you can select the corresponding images and labels.
Choose image_sequences, then field_A01, as the image folder. Select channel zero: each example image contains one cell-intensity channel. Set Frames previewed to eight and Fields to one.

Click Masks and select label_sequences, then field_A01. Each label identifies an object in the corresponding image. Leave Keep only full-length tracks off initially so you can inspect tracks that start or end within the sequence.

Set the overlap threshold to zero point one and click Run preview. This threshold controls how much adjacent masks must overlap to be linked. Inspect the coloured object identities and the track-length summary. The example produces sixteen tracks spanning all eight frames.

Adjust the overlap threshold if objects split into short tracks or link to the wrong neighbours. A higher threshold requires more overlap. After changing it, wait for the preview to finish and click Re-link to inspect the final value. Scrub through several frames before accepting the result.
Use the frame slider to follow the same object across the sequence. Play changes how quickly you view the frames. Keep the actual acquisition interval separately for later speed measurements.

For a full run on your own images, set Source and the intensity channels in Mask. Here, import the settings of the small synthetic eight-frame example. Keep each field’s timepoints in order. Frame limits use a start and an excluded end: zero to eight selects the first eight frames.

Choose the object to track and the tracking mode. The overlap mode, iou, links objects using their masks in adjacent frames. Inspect a short sequence first and choose a mode suited to how far your objects move between frames.
Turn on Keep original images to retain the input images during pipeline cleanup. Set the segmentation model and channels for your data, and check the preview before processing the full sequence.

Turn on Plot to inspect the generated figures, then click Run. Follow progress in the console and wait for completion. Begin with a short sequence so you can check the masks and track identities before processing a larger experiment.

Inspect the intensity and label planes in the output figures. The run saves tracked arrays in merged and track tables in tracks under the project folder. Continue to Measure, then Motility, to calculate object features and movement from those tracks.

lessons.title: Train a Cellpose model
lessons.description: Prepare image/mask pairs, fine-tune a segmentation model in the Cellpose Workbench and apply the saved checkpoint.
objectives: Inspect matching images and object-label masks in Make Masks.
Choose the training folder, starting model, schedule and output location.
Run training, find the checkpoint and apply it to separate images.
lessons.prerequisite: Download and extract the linked example: six training images with masks, plus three separate images for Apply. Or prepare your own images and matching integer-label masks, and inspect them in Make Masks before training.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Tools, then Make Masks. Open Cellpose Workbench from its toolbar; it starts on the Train tab. You will train from images and their object-label masks, then use the saved model in Apply.

Extract the linked example. Its training folder holds six images and a masks subfolder, and its apply folder holds three separate images for later. Click the folder button beside Image source folder and choose training. Leave Mask source folder empty to use the masks subfolder, or choose another folder of masks.

Each image needs one mask with the same height and width. Zero is background, and each object has its own positive number. Open the training folder in Make Masks to inspect the labels and correct them before training. This image has ninety-five labelled cells.

This example is grayscale, so leave Channels empty. For a multichannel image, add up to three zero-based channel numbers, such as zero and two for the first and third channels. Set Channel axis only if automatic detection cannot find the channel dimension.

Keep Base model at cpsam to start from Cellpose-SAM, or enter a checkpoint path to continue training an earlier model. Enter a Model name; here it is tutorial cells. Leave Checkpoint folder empty to save inside the source folder, or choose another folder.

Set N epochs and Batch size. This quick run uses ten epochs with a batch size of one. More epochs give the model more training updates, and larger batches use more memory. Keep the displayed learning rate to begin.

Keep Normalize on, with the first and ninety-ninth percentiles as a starting point. These set the intensity range used for each channel. Scale range varies the image size during training, and Min train masks skips images with fewer labelled objects.

To follow validation loss, choose a separate Validation image folder and its Validation mask folder. Never reuse training images there. Leave both empty when you have no separate labelled set, as in this example.
Check the folders, model name and output location, then press Run. The Figures panel shows the training images above their masks, and the console follows progress.

When training finishes, the console gives the checkpoint path. With the default location it is in the source folder, under models, cellpose model, models. The file name adds the architecture and epoch count to your model name. Keep it with your training settings.

Open the Apply tab. Custom model now points to the checkpoint you trained. Set Source to the example apply folder, whose images come from wells that were not used for training. Set Channels to zero and Percentiles to two and ninety-nine. Turn off Fill in so touching cells stay separate, and turn on Save and Verbose.

Open Live preview, choose one image and press Run preview, with the same channel and percentiles. It segments that image with your checkpoint, here finding seventy-eight cells. Adjust settings here before running the whole folder.

Press Run. Apply writes one mask per image into a masks subfolder beside those images, and Verbose shows each result as a figure. Here the three masks hold seventy-nine, fifty and fifty-five cells. Before using a model on a whole experiment, compare its masks with separately labelled fields.

lessons.title: Apply Cellpose: segment a folder and inspect masks
lessons.description: Choose a segmentation model, process the supplied images and inspect saved masks and live size filters.
objectives: Select images, model weights and segmentation settings.
Run Apply and locate the saved mask TIFFs.
Inspect live results and compare object-size filters.
lessons.prerequisite: Extract the linked Apply Cellpose example into a new folder. It contains three single-channel cell images and a settings reference. Select its images folder as Source. This walkthrough uses the stock cpsam model; for a custom model, choose compatible weights and settings for your images.
