Click Open crops for the selected family. Annotate opens only the matching parent-cell crop and reports two unavailable child crops. This example includes cell crops only; nucleus and pathogen crops are not available.
Double-click the parent cell in Lineage. Annotate opens that parent’s matching cell crop. This is the crop available in the downloaded example.
Shift-click the parent thumbnail to enlarge its preview, then press Escape to return. An ordinary left click assigns an annotation class, so use Shift when you only want to inspect.

Click Build tree to refresh the view. For the full hierarchy in Python, use read_object_tables, build_forest and lineage_frame, then save the frame as CSV. The linked example CSV contains all seven thousand two hundred one nodes.

lessons.title: Graph Builder: plot measurements and filter objects
lessons.description: Load a measurement table, compare groups, filter objects and build illustrative genotype, replicate and combined condition columns.
objectives: Load an example measurement table.
Build a histogram, scatter plot and grouped panels.
Filter objects and choose a follow-up view.
Assign exact-value labels in separate output columns and combine them without changing source measurements.
Extract text into columns, save and load an annotation schema, and merge tables.
lessons.prerequisite: Download and extract Graph_Builder_real_measurements.zip. It contains measurements.db. To inspect image crops later, also keep the matching Annotate project and its images available.

scenes.narration: Open Graph Builder from Home to explore a measurement table. Start with the linked example database, then repeat the steps with your own measured project.

Click Load table and open measurements dot db from the extracted archive. Choose the cell table. This example contains two thousand three hundred forty-one measured cells. Merge tables, beside the table picker, combines several tables into one; we use it at the end.
Find cell_area in the column list and drag it onto X. The automatic chart becomes a histogram: each bar counts cells in an area interval. Check the measurement units before interpreting the axis.
Drag cell_channel_1_mean_intensity onto Y to make a scatter plot. Each point places one cell by its area and channel-one mean intensity. Read the row-count notice when working with larger tables.
Drag columnID onto Colour to distinguish plate columns. Use the legend to match colours to the recorded column labels and look for groups that need closer inspection.

Drag rowID onto the downward facet channel to create a panel for each plate row. Compare the panels using their shared axes. Use independent wells when making statistical comparisons between conditions.

In the filter panel on the right, add cell_area and enter a minimum. The example uses twenty-one thousand nine hundred twenty-five, leaving one thousand one hundred seventy-one rows. Choose thresholds appropriate to your own measurements and watch the plotted count and axes change.
Click Clear all in the filter panel to restore the full table. Use Clear all channels on the left when you want to remove the plot mappings and start a different chart.

Clear all channels keeps the plot kind but removes every column from the chart, and the canvas then says what is missing: drag a column onto X or Y to draw a chart again. Drop the same columns back to continue.

Remove a facet with its small cross to return to one scatter plot. Drag a rectangle around objects to select a region. If Open selection in Annotate is unavailable, open Annotate separately with the matching project and inspect objects there.
Click an empty part of the plot to clear the selection. Check the active filters and displayed count before exploring another group of objects.

Click Annotate conditions. Name the first output genotype and use Assign values. Choose Exact values, then label columnID values c1, c2 and c3 as WildType. Add a second box named mutant for c7, c4, c5 and c6. These are illustrative labels, not validated genotypes. The downloaded table contains only c1 and c2, so every cell matches WildType and none matches mutant. Exact values match whole values: c1 does not match c10.

Add an output column named replicate. Match rowID values r1, r4, r5 and r6 in a box named replicate 1. Add another box with the same name for r7, r9 and r10. Boxes with the same label form a union; conflicting different labels in one output must be resolved before Apply conditions. The example contains r5 and r12, so r5 matches and r12 remains blank. These practice labels do not establish biological replication.

Add a third output named condition and choose Compose column. Select genotype under Available columns and click Add column token. Enter an underscore and click Add text token. Select replicate and click Add column token. The ordered tokens now read genotype, underscore, replicate. You can drag tokens or use Move token up and Move token down to change their order. Preview all three outputs. Matched r5 cells become WildType underscore replicate 1. A missing component leaves the combination blank, so r12 does not produce a label containing None or nan.

An output can also be extracted from text. Add a fourth output named row_number and choose Extract text. Pick rowID as the source column and enter a regular expression with a named group, here r followed by a group called row_number that captures the digits. Click Create columns from named groups, then Preview. Rows that do not match stay blank. The example table has no original filenames, so we extract from an existing ID column.

Click Save schema and choose a JSON file. A schema keeps the rules, not the values: the outputs, their boxes, compositions and extraction patterns. Manual row assignments are tied to this table and are left out, and the status line says how many were omitted.
Load schema reads such a file onto the same or another table. It is checked against the table's columns and opens as a preview of every output; nothing is applied until you click Apply conditions.

Select genotype under Generated columns to check what the schema restored: the WildType and mutant boxes return with their exact values, and each box shows how many rows it matches. Check every output this way before you click Apply conditions.

Click Apply conditions to add genotype, replicate, condition and row_number to the working table. The original measurement columns and source database remain unchanged. The same annotation editor also works with a merged working table. Use your experimental design to choose meaningful labels before plotting by these new columns.

Save chart preserves the view and annotation recipe for reloading. Export table includes the generated columns. For a SQLite source, Save annotated table asks for a new table name, suggesting cell_annotated, and never overwrites an existing table. These are separate persistence actions; Apply conditions alone does not write the source database.

To combine tables, click Merge tables beside the table picker. Tick cell, nucleus and pathogen, keep cell as the output observation table so there is one row per cell, and name the result. Click Validate and preview and read the row counts and join keys for each table, then click Create merged table.

The merged table is selected in the picker and its columns can be plotted like any other. The source tables in the database are unchanged; the merge is saved as a reproducible definition beside the database.
Use the header shortcuts to open Plate Viewer for well heatmaps or Small Multiples for repeated charts. Keep the source database and your chosen columns and filters so you can reproduce the view.

lessons.title: Feature Dictionary: find definitions and units
lessons.description: Search by measurement name or concept, read the definition and units, and copy useful reference text.
objectives: Find a definition by name or concept.
Narrow the results with concept and object filters.
Read units and notes, then copy the definition.
lessons.prerequisite: Have a measurement column name ready, or start with an idea such as size or intensity. The built-in dictionary can be opened without loading a project.

scenes.narration: Open Help, then Feature Dictionary. Use this window when you want to understand a measurement column in a results table or plot.
Type size in the search field and select Area from the results. The definition appears on the right, and the matching list updates as you type.
Choose a concept and object type to narrow the definitions. Try intensity and cell. Reset the selectors to Any concept and Any object for a broader search.
Search for cell_channel_1_mean_intensity and select Mean intensity. Read the statistic and units to understand what the column describes.
Scroll down to Channel, Module and Computed by for more detail. Use the named computing function as a starting point in the API reference.

Look up cell_area and read Unit. In two-dimensional measurements it represents area; in three-dimensional measurements it represents volume. Check the measurement units recorded in your project before converting values.

Read Note for qualifications such as values already expressed in physical units. For a dictionary of the columns actually present in a database, use describe_database and export_dictionary from Python.
If no definitions match, clear the filters and try a broader term or the exact column name. Custom features may need documentation from the workflow that created them.
Select the definition text and copy it into your notes. Use the Python export functions when you need a project-specific dictionary file, then return to your table or plot.

lessons.title: Small Multiples: compare groups with shared or separate axes
lessons.description: Load measurements, arrange grouped scatter plots, choose axis scales and filters, and add a derived column.
objectives: Load measurements and assign axes and facets.
Choose shared, independent or grouped axis limits.
Inspect filters and displayed groups, then add or remove a derived column.
lessons.prerequisite: Download the measurement example from the Annotate tutorial and work with a copy of measurements.db. This walkthrough uses its cell table, with 2,341 objects across four wells. Small Multiples displays plots; use Tabulate to export grouped CSV summaries.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Graph Builder, then Small Multiples. Use this view to compare the same measurements across groups. This example uses the measurements database available from the linked Annotate tutorial.

Click Load table beside the Small Multiples heading. Open a copy of measurements.db and select cell. Check the table and its two thousand three hundred forty-one objects before assigning plot channels.

Drag cell_area onto X and cell_channel_1_mean_intensity onto Y, then choose Scatter. Put rowID on Facet down and columnID on Facet across. Search helps you find column names; each point represents a measured cell.
Choose shared for both scales so all four panels use matching axis limits. Read the group titles and object counts. In this example the facet labels identify spatial rows and columns.
Choose free for X scale and Y scale to give each panel its own limits. This makes within-group patterns easier to see. Compare tick labels carefully because the ranges now differ between panels.
Choose per row for both scales to share limits between panels on each grid row. Different rows can have different ranges. Use this when comparisons within rows are the priority.
Choose per column to share limits within each grid column. You can set X and Y independently. Restore shared on both axes when you want to compare all four wells on common scales.

In Filter, add cell_area and set its minimum to twenty-one thousand nine hundred twenty-five. The grid updates immediately for the remaining one thousand one hundred seventy-one objects. Check the new panel counts.

Click Clear all in Filter to restore the full population. Use Clear all channels on the left when you want to remove the chart assignments instead. Both operations leave the source database unchanged.

Filter columnID to c two and fieldID to f twenty and f twenty-one. Put fieldID on Facet across and keep rowID on Facet down. The row-five, field-twenty panel has no objects; its empty panel represents a missing group.
Clear the filters and restore columnID on Facet across. Set Wrap at to five. Wrapping applies to a single facet channel, so the current two-way grid stays two by two.
Clear Facet down and put fieldID on Facet across. With Wrap at five, the displayed fields fill rows of up to five panels. Unused slots at the end are hidden.

Read the notice below the grid before comparing groups. This view displays twelve field levels; field twenty-one is omitted from the panels. The loaded-row count includes that field, so check which groups are actually visible.

Turn wrapping off and restore rowID and columnID as the two facets. In Columns, name a derived column area_k and enter cell_area divided by one thousand. Check the preview, then click Add column to compute it for the full table.

Drag area_k onto X to display area in thousands of the original units. The vertical coordinates and groups stay the same. This rescales numbers; physical-area conversion requires the correct image calibration.
Put cell_area back on X. Select area_k in Columns and click Remove to delete the derived column from this view. Keep a record of your variables, facets, filters and scale choices.

Use Tabulate when you need an exported CSV summary. For scripted small-multiple plots, use trellis and TrellisSpec from spacr.qt.widgets.trellis_spec with GraphSpec for the chart channels. Interpret the groups at the appropriate experimental replicate level.

lessons.title: Gate Editor: select populations and save their membership
lessons.description: Draw gates on measurements, save reusable boundaries, explore projections and export object membership to a database.
objectives: Load measurements and draw named gates.
Save and reload gate strategies, figures and membership.
Explore three-dimensional views, clustering and filters.
lessons.prerequisite: Download the Annotate example and make a working copy of measurements.db. Gate Editor uses its 2,341 cell measurements; it has no separate example-download button. Export gates writes membership to the chosen database. Gate names should describe the selected measurements until their biological meaning has been established.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Tools and choose Gate Editor. Adjust the dividers so you can see the plot, gate table and side controls. Use the measurement database from the Annotate example.

Click Load table, open your working copy of measurements.db and choose cell. The example contains two thousand three hundred forty-one objects. Keep a copy because Export gates writes membership to this database. Merge tables, beside the picker, combines the cell table with its nucleus or pathogen tables into one new table, as in Graph Builder; the source tables stay unchanged.
Choose cell_area for X and cell_channel_1_mean_intensity for Y, then select Rectangle. Each point represents an object. Check the feature names and units before drawing.
Drag across the scatter, release and enter a descriptive gate name. The gate stores boundaries in the two selected measurements.

Read the count and percentage beside the gate name. The illustrated region contains six hundred fifty-five objects. Your mouse positions may give different boundaries; save a strategy to repeat an exact selection.
Untick the gate to hide its overlay, then tick it to show it again. Delete gate removes its definition. The Filter tab separately controls the objects displayed beneath the gates.
Click Save gates to write a JSON strategy. Delete the gate, then choose Load gates and open the saved file. Reuse strategies with matching feature names, units and preprocessing.
The loaded strategy restores the saved boundaries and population. Check the axes, outline and count before continuing with another dataset.
Choose Save graph to save the plotted figure. File formats follow your plotting preferences; this example produces PNG and PDF. Keep the JSON strategy beside the figure.
Choose Export gates to write membership flags to the working database’s filters table. Each flag is associated with the object’s plate, well, field, label and type.
Draw a second gate and give it a new name. New shapes are independent of the selected gate, so the second can include objects outside the first. Save this two-gate strategy under a new filename.
Choose three D and set Z to cell_perimeter. Use the spin-axis buttons to rotate the view. Return to two D to inspect the original area-intensity boundaries.
Use From view to create a named box bounded by the three displayed measurements. Check its population count and save the new strategy separately.
Choose Free under spin to orbit the volume: drag sideways and up and down at once, and the view stays exactly where you let go. Turn it until the population you want stands apart from the rest.

Choose Polygon through view and switch drag to Draw. Click the corners around the population on screen; the status line counts the vertices, and the outline is swept through the whole volume at the angle you see.

Click the first corner again to close the polygon and name the gate; here it holds one thousand four hundred seventy-nine objects. Double-click any gate in the gate table to rename it; its child gates follow the new name.
Enable x D to compute principal components from eligible measurements. The axis labels show explained variance for each component. Choose two D or three D separately to control the view.

When turning x D off, select the raw measurement axes again. Save projection details separately: the gate JSON does not retain the fitted projection, and component boundaries may differ between independently fitted datasets.

Open Search and widen its panel. Save and remove temporary gates, choose the two raw features, enable scaling and set twenty minimum neighbours and five Walk steps. Click Run walk and review the confirmation values.
Inspect the resulting outlines and population counts. Here Walk chooses a radius near zero point one six seven and finds two populations. Review which objects lie outside those regions.
Save the Walk strategy, remove its gates and switch Walk off. Try radius zero point five to compare the resulting larger region, then choose the strategy appropriate to your analysis.
Reload the saved two-gate strategy. In Filter, add cell_area with a minimum of twenty-one thousand nine hundred twenty-five. The view now contains one thousand one hundred seventy-one objects.
Click Clear all to restore the full population. Check the active filters and gate definitions before interpreting counts or exporting membership.
To inspect the loaded table directly, open the right-hand console and enter len(df). This example returns two thousand three hundred forty-one rows.
Keep your data, JSON strategy and exported membership together. In Python, use GateSet for definitions, gate_mask_over_table to calculate membership and export_gate to save object flags.

lessons.title: Experiment Design: plan a plate and export its well map
lessons.description: Set conditions and replicates, choose a layout, review warnings and export assignments for acquisition and analysis.
objectives: Enter conditions, replicate counts and control roles.
Choose a plate format, edge policy and reproducible random layout.
Export the exact well assignments for later joins to measurements.
lessons.prerequisite: Prepare your condition names, control roles and intended well counts before acquisition. The example requests six negative-control wells, six positive-control wells and twelve treatment wells; choose replication for your own experiment. Keep the plate identifier consistent with later images and measurements.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Data and choose Experiment Design. Start by entering the conditions and controls you want to place on the plate.
Name the plate using the identifier you will use during acquisition. Review Condition, Replicates and Role in the table. Double-click a column boundary to widen it when needed.

Choose a plate format with enough wells for the requested replicates. Selecting six wells for this twenty-four-well plan displays a capacity error. Change the format or the requested counts to continue.
Select ninety-six wells to restore the layout. Use Add condition and Remove selected to edit condition rows, then check the updated plate map.
To edit a replicate count, select its cell and press F two. A single negative-control well triggers a warning. Choose independent experimental replication appropriate to your analysis.
Choose Block layout to group conditions together. Read the positional warnings and inspect the map for potential confounding between condition and position.
Choose Random layout, enable Leave edge empty and set Seed to forty-two. This ninety-six-well plate has sixty interior wells available, with twenty-four assigned by the example plan.
Change Seed to forty-three to generate another arrangement with the same condition counts. Review the placement of controls and treatments across the plate.
Restore Seed forty-two to recover the previous arrangement. Save the seed together with the format, edge policy and condition table.
Drag across wells B zero two to C zero four to select them. This selects wells for inspection; use the condition table and layout controls to change assignments.
Click Export plate map and choose a folder. Keep plate_map.csv, plate_map.json and plate_map_settings.json together.
Open the CSV to inspect one row per assigned well. Join it to later measurements using plateID, rowID and columnID together. The JSON retains the design and its warnings.

For this randomized layout, the settings file reports expressible as false. Use the exact CSV well map for condition labels: whole-row or whole-column treatment settings cannot represent these mixed assignments.

Review the final map before acquisition and retain it with the experiment. In Python, use Condition and PlateDesign, followed by assign_wells, check_design and write_design from spacr.qt.widgets.plate_layout.

lessons.title: Explain CV Model: compare predictions with measured features
lessons.description: Load matching predictions and measurements, fit a surrogate and read fidelity before using feature explanations.
objectives: Match the measurement database to saved classifier predictions.
Choose prediction columns, a backend and held-out groups.
Read fidelity, confusion and saved feature summaries.
lessons.prerequisite: Use measurements.db and the predictions CSV from the same Annotate/Classify example objects. Select the saved model class calls as the target. This example has limited surrogate fidelity, so its feature attributions should not be used to explain the vision model. Evaluate the original classifier separately with independent data.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Classify, then choose Explain CV Model at the upper right. Prepare the measurement database and saved predictions for the same cropped objects.
Select measurements.db and the matching predictions CSV. Check the filenames and object identities before continuing. This example uses two hundred thirty-four saved predictions.

Confirm the prediction path with Enter if the column choices have not refreshed. Choose filename for the crop path and predicted_label for the model’s class calls. Select Random Forest, grouping by well and a new output folder.
Click Explain model. The surrogate uses measured features to reproduce the saved class calls. Choose the backend and grouping on this form; use the Python API for additional fitting options.

Read Fidelity first. Here eighty-nine rows have complete features, with sixty-eight used for fitting and twenty-one from another well held out. Compare agreement with the baseline and inspect which rows were excluded.

Open Importance. In this example the fidelity gate withholds the ranking. Review the excluded feature names as well: a name-based leakage warning needs to be checked against what the measurement actually contains.

Open Confusion to compare surrogate calls with the vision model’s calls. Here every held-out object is assigned class one, giving seventeen agreements and four differences. Check performance across classes rather than relying only on overall agreement.
Per-cell SHAP describes the fitted surrogate. When fidelity is inadequate, these values cannot explain the vision model reliably. Keep that limitation with any exported attribution table.
Open Correlations and Feature distributions to inspect the measurements. These GUI tables show up to one thousand rows. Use their saved CSV files to inspect the full summaries.

Open Held-out cells to see object identities and both predictions. Keep the output files, settings and fidelity report together. Continue with the Evaluation tutorial when you need to assess the original classifier.

lessons.title: Import Images: map image identities and create a project
lessons.description: Scan image names and metadata, review the proposed well/field/channel mapping, save a plan and import copies into a project.
objectives: Scan microscope images and resolve naming questions.
Choose a destination, plate name and copy or link behavior.
Save a reusable plan and import images for Mask.
lessons.prerequisite: Download the Mask example first. Use working copies of fields E01/F001 and L01/F009, with four channels each. In those copies only, remove the redundant A token immediately before Z, preserving every well, field and channel token. Keep the originals and use acquisition records when resolving unfamiliar tokens.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Data, choose Import, then Import Images. Start with the microscope image files you want to organize into a project.

When you also have masks, click Organize images and masks beside the image folder. Drop each channel folder and the mask folder into their columns, set the mask's role, and under Write for choose Mask Generation or Measure. Files with several channels can be split into one column per channel first; Apply moves everything into that module's layout and records each move in a manifest.
Use the Mask example for this walkthrough. Select copies of one field from each of two wells, with four channels per field. Keep the original download unchanged.
Click Scan. If it asks what a filename token means, check the acquisition records before assigning it. Continue only when the proposed identities distinguish the fields and channels unambiguously.

Scan those working copies. Their redundant acquisition token has been removed, while the well, field and channel tokens remain. Check that the proposal lists eight images, two wells, two field numbers and four channels.
Compare the proposal with the filenames. Enable Read inside each file when you need embedded axis metadata. Set Sample large enough to inspect the files you intend to import.

Choose a destination outside the input folder and enter the plate name. Turn Link instead of copy off for independent copies. Links save disk space but require the original files to remain accessible.

For tiled acquisitions, choose whether to stitch, retain separate tiles or skip them. Review the resulting field organization before measuring. These example images are separate fields, so they do not need stitching.
Click Save plan to retain the source and mapping choices as JSON. Keep the plan with the acquisition notes and original images.
Click Load plan to reload the source and saved answers. Review the new proposal before importing, especially when the source files have changed.
Click Import and read the summary. This example produces eight image copies with no skipped files. Open the resulting project in Mask and inspect Live preview before starting segmentation.

lessons.title: spaCR screens
lessons.description: Follow a pooled image-based screen from Home through image measurements, phenotype classification, barcode counts and regression.
objectives: Choose a starting module from the data you already have.
Identify what each module reads and writes.
Follow the linked module lessons and API contracts for the next step.
lessons.prerequisite: Install spaCR and open Home. Choose the starting data for your workflow, then follow the linked module lessons for controls and example data.

scenes.narration: A pooled screen tells its story twice, once in images and once in sequencing reads, and spaCR brings the two together at the end. On the image side, Mask and Measure turn your microscope fields into measured cells, and Annotate and Classify turn those cells into phenotype scores. On the sequencing side, Map Barcodes turns reads into guide counts. Regression joins the two by plate and well. Join wherever your results begin.

Everything starts with your microscope images. Open Mask from Home, choose the channels and a segmentation model, and check the preview before you run it. Mask finds the objects in every field and saves each field as a merged array, the image channels stacked with their label masks. Those merged arrays are what Measure opens next. The small counts database Mask leaves behind is only a tally, not yet a feature table.

Next, open Measure from Home and point it at the same project, with the image and mask channel indices set correctly. Measure reads each merged array, images and label planes together, and writes every cell, nucleus or parasite as a row in measurements.db. Turn on crop saving and it also cuts a small PNG around each object, indexed in png_list. From here the story forks. Annotate shows those crops so you can label examples, and Classify learns from either the crops or the measured features, so keep object identities stable.

Before a classifier can learn anything, it needs examples. Open Annotate from Home to view the object crops associated with your measured project. Click through representative cells and label them. Each label is written to an annotation column in the png_list table, tied to that object's identity. Use a separate column for each question, and set some labelled objects aside for evaluation. That annotation column is what Classify trains on next.

Open Classify from Home, and here your labels become scores. Classify has two families, and your data picks between them. Computer Vision learns from the object crops themselves, while Tabular Machine Learning learns from the measured feature columns. Either way, it trains on the labels you made in Annotate, checks itself on the objects you held out, and saves the trained model, an evaluation bundle and the scores, as CSV files and, when merged, in png_list. Pick the CV or ML score column you mean to test, keep plate and well identity intact, and carry it into Regression.

While the images go one way, the sequencing reads go another. Open Map Barcodes from Home, give it your FASTQ files and the barcode references that encode your screen, and it counts which guides turned up in each well. Check the mapped counts and barcode QC before you trust them. The unique_combinations.csv it writes is the guide-count table Regression pairs with your phenotype scores, well by well.

This is where the two halves of the screen meet. Open Regression from Home and give it both: the phenotype scores from Classify and the guide counts from Map Barcodes. Regression matches them on plate and well, so those keys have to agree in both files. Choose the response column and your controls, run the fit, and open the diagnostics before you believe any hit. If your barcodes were read optically with OPS instead, join and aggregate the decoded objects to your phenotype and guide data first; OPS does not hand over a ready-made count table. Regression can also model a directly measured response. It writes a results folder of coefficients, hit tables, settings and diagnostic figures.

So a pooled screen runs as two streams that meet in Regression. Before you open it, check that the plate and well identifiers match across your scores, guide counts and plate layout, and keep the annotation column, classifier settings and barcode references with the run. The linked module lessons walk through each step, or choose the pooled-screen walkthrough on Home.

lessons.title: Image analysis modules and how they relate
lessons.description: Follow the current image-to-measurement routes and choose exploration, labeling, comparison or organism-specific analyses.
objectives: Choose a starting module from the data you already have.
Identify what each module reads and writes.
Follow the linked module lessons and API contracts for the next step.
lessons.prerequisite: Install spaCR and open Home. Choose the starting data for your workflow, then follow the linked module lessons for controls and example data.

scenes.narration: Start with the question and the data you already have. The current Home rows separate Core analysis, Data preparation and comparison, Tools, and the Toxoplasma Organism page. A module is one step; its output becomes another module’s input.

Import organizes incoming microscopy files and metadata. If your acquisition contains overlapping tiles, Align & Stitch can prepare a mosaic with its coordinate records. Keep channel identities and source metadata with the project.

Mask produces object labels from microscopy images. Make Masks lets you create or review masks manually. Image-mask pairs must keep the same field identity; a loose mask file is not automatically the combined project arrays Measure needs.

Measure reads the prepared images and mask planes together. It writes measurements.db with object identities and feature columns, and can save object crops. Keep the source project and channel mapping with those tables.

Annotate displays object crops so you can add reviewed labels. Classify trains a model on the selected label column, using crop images or measured features. Keep evaluation objects separate from training objects and carry the score column and object identities into later analyses.

Embeddings encodes crops into numerical features. Image UMAP projects compatible features for exploration. Inspect representative crops before assigning meaning to a cluster; a cluster alone is not a validated phenotype.

Gate Editor selects objects using real feature columns or compatible projection coordinates. Review the selected objects before writing labels. Those labels can become reviewed examples for Annotate or Classify.

QC reports the quality checks that are present and the evidence that is missing. Run Compare inspects saved runs side by side. Graph Builder plots measurement tables with the columns and grouping you choose.

Experiment Design plans conditions and sample identities. Power / Design explores statistical planning assumptions. Dose-Response analyzes an endpoint across concentrations. Keep the measurement endpoint, controls and experimental unit explicit.

The Toxoplasma page groups organism-specific assays. Their inputs differ: a plaque image, compartment measurements or explicit parasite-to-vacuole links are not interchangeable. Choose the matching assay and follow its own input requirements.

For pooled screens, Map Barcodes produces guide counts from sequencing reads. Regression combines those counts with compatible phenotype scores. Preserve plate, well and guide identity when joining the two routes.

Return Home and choose the next step from the output you actually have. Use the linked module lessons for a complete run. Keep the input identity, settings, installed version and output location together so the workflow can be checked later.

lessons.title: Sequencing modules and how they relate
lessons.description: Connect sequencing and optical barcode workflows to phenotype scores, regression, experiment planning, power estimates, dose-response analysis and run comparison.
objectives: Choose a starting module from the data you already have.
Identify what each module reads and writes.
Follow the linked module lessons and API contracts for the next step.
lessons.prerequisite: Install spaCR and open Home. Choose the starting data for your workflow, then follow the linked module lessons for controls and example data.

scenes.narration: Sequencing is how a pooled screen learns which guide sits in which well or cell, and spaCR reads it two ways. Reads from a sequencer go into Map Barcodes. Barcodes imaged cycle by cycle go into OPS, which lives inside Mask. Either way, the barcode identities end up beside your phenotypes in Regression. Around that core sit the planning tools, Experiment Design and Power, for before you acquire, and Dose–Response and Run Compare for your results.

Start with the sequencing reads. Open Map Barcodes from Home and give it your FASTQ files, single-end or paired, with the barcode reference tables that encode your experiment. Map Barcodes matches each read to its barcodes and counts the guides in every well, saving unique_combinations.csv and annotated_reads.h5 in its run folder. Before you trust those counts, open them in Barcode QC. Once they pass, they are the guide counts Regression pairs with phenotype scores, on the same plate and well keys.

Barcode QC lives inside Map Barcodes, so open Map Barcodes from Home and choose it there. It reads the guide counts you just made and shows mapping depth, coverage, barcode collisions and positional effects. It saves the QC results with exportable figures and tables, so you can decide which guides to filter before going further.

Optical screens take a different road. Open Mask from Home, then choose OPS. Instead of reads, OPS takes the images from each sequencing cycle, aligns them to the phenotype images and decodes a barcode for every nucleus. The results land in the OPS measurements.db, with tables for geometry, phenotype alignment, nuclei and barcodes. That database is not a FASTQ count table, though. To use it in Regression, first join and aggregate the decoded identities with your phenotype data, so each object or well carries both.

Whichever way you sequenced, barcodes meet phenotypes in Regression. Open it from Home. For a pooled screen, it takes phenotype scores from Classify and guide counts from Map Barcodes. For an optical screen, it takes the decoded OPS objects once you have joined and aggregated them yourself; that is not a direct file handoff. It can also model a directly measured response. In every case, plate and well identifiers must agree across the inputs. Choose the response and the controls, run the fit, and read the diagnostics before you call anything a hit. The results folder it writes, with coefficients, hit tables, settings and figures, is what Run Compare opens when you want to line this run up against another.

Now step back to before the experiment. Open Power / Design from Home to estimate how much sampling you need to see an effect, based on the effect sizes and variability you choose. Pilot measurements can support those assumptions, but they are optional. The layout from Experiment Design feeds these estimates, and the estimates in turn may send you back to revise that design.

Open Experiment Design from Home to lay out the plates before you acquire anything. Enter the conditions, controls, replicates and plate constraints, with your power estimates in mind, and export the experimental layout. That layout travels far. Power / Design uses it to set sampling assumptions, and later, once the experiment is acquired and measured, Dose–Response uses its dose and condition identities, so keep them unchanged all the way through.

Dose–Response answers how much, not which guide, so it needs no sequencing at all. Open it from Home and bring your measured responses with the dose and condition identities from Experiment Design. Set the dose and response columns, controls and units, then fit the curves. It saves assay results with figures and tables to export.

Once you have more than one analysis, open Run Compare from Home. It reads your saved run records and Regression results and sets their settings, counts and hit lists side by side. If the input data changed between runs, the differences are not a controlled model comparison, so read them with that in mind.

One more planning tool lives only in Python: the pooled-screen simulation sweep, spacr.sim.run_multiple_simulations, with no Home tile or menu entry. You give it a settings dictionary of assumptions, such as screen size, occupancy, classifier accuracy and sequencing. It expands every combination, simulates each in a process pool and appends synthetic summary rows to simulations.db; the call itself returns None. Keep the parameter grid small and set max_workers explicitly before you run it. What comes out is planning evidence, not data, and it cannot stand in for measurements or barcode counts in Regression. Read the summaries, record your assumptions, and carry them by hand into Power / Design or Experiment Design, since neither tool imports the simulation database.

So the barcode side of a screen always ends the same way: identities joined to phenotypes by plate and well. Keep barcode references and plate layouts with your count tables, and for an optical screen, join the decoded objects to their phenotypes and aggregate them before Regression. The linked module lessons show the settings and outputs for each step.

lessons.title: Toxoplasma organism: guide, diagram and assays
lessons.description: Open the organism page, explore the cell diagram and choose an available assay.
objectives: Open the page from Home and find its main controls.
Identify the available inputs, actions and outputs.
Choose the next available analysis or reference.
lessons.prerequisite: Open spaCR Home. The organism guide requires no input files. Each assay has its own inputs and linked walkthrough.

scenes.narration: From Home, choose the Organism category, then Toxoplasma. This page combines an organism guide, an interactive cell diagram and the available Toxoplasma assay routes. Explore it before choosing an analysis.
Begin with the introduction in the information pane. Each pane scrolls on its own, and dragging the divider gives the guide or the assay tiles more room.
The diagram is interactive. Hover over a cell component and its description appears. Select several to keep them highlighted, and Clear components resets the picture.

Plaque Assay counts plaques and measures their areas. Recruitment measures marker enrichment at the parasite-containing vacuole, and Replication Assay counts parasites per vacuole. Select an assay according to the quantity you need to measure and its required input.

Click Plaque Assay to open its analysis screen. The settings panel specifies the image source, masks and detection options. Load test data provides an example. Review the inputs and preview before starting Run; the Plaque Assay tutorial describes the complete workflow.

Return to the Toxoplasma guide and scroll the information pane to its references. ToxoDB, the Toxoplasma hyperLOPIT atlas, UniProt and NCBI Taxonomy link to organism resources. These links open in your browser; the guide does not perform a database search or predict protein localization.

The organism guide does not produce analysis tables. Return Home for image preparation, segmentation or measurement, then choose the assay that matches your prepared input. Each assay has its own requirements and linked walkthrough.

lessons.title: Host–Pathogen: link vacuole markers and parasite counts
lessons.description: Load the microscopy example, choose marker and count inputs, inspect the preview, and export linked vacuole, host-cell and well summaries.
objectives: Load the example project and identify the host and vacuole measurements.
Choose marker channels and inspect vacuole-level recruitment in Live preview.
Run the analysis and read the output tables with the correct denominators.
lessons.prerequisite: Use Load test data for the supplied THP-1 microscopy example, or select a measured project with host cells, vacuoles and host-reference intensities. Retain uninfected host cells during Measure when you need an infection denominator. Individual parasite counts require a linked parasite table or a measured count column.

scenes.narration: Host–Pathogen ties every vacuole's markers and parasite count back to its host cell and its well. To get there, open Toxoplasma from Home, then choose Host–Pathogen.

The easiest way in is the example. Load test data downloads a small microscopy project and fills in the settings: two fields with images, host and vacuole masks, and measurement tables. Practise here before switching to your own measured project.

Everything the module reads comes through Source, which should point at the project holding measurements/measurements.db. It can also read a database directly, or combine several projects while keeping each one's identity separate.

Now tell it where vacuoles and hosts live in that database: the vacuole table and its intensity-column prefix, then the host-reference table and its prefix. The example uses pathogen and cytoplasm. The object links connect each vacuole to its host cell, so check they are right.

Marker channels says which intensities to compare, counted from zero. The example picks channel one, the RNF213 marker. Whatever you pick needs intensity measurements in both the vacuole and the reference compartment, because the ratio is built from the two.

At first, leave Marker thresholds empty and simply look at the recruitment ratios. Once your controls show where positive begins, enter the channel number and that ratio threshold; anything at or above it counts as positive. If a reference measurement is missing or invalid, the state stays unknown rather than guessed.

Parasite counts come from one of two places: a parasite table whose rows link to their parent vacuole, or a count column measured on each vacuole. The microscopy example has neither, so leave both empty here, and its parasite counts and replication readouts stay unknown.

Before running everything, try one field. Turn on Live, choose a field and click Run preview. The vacuole table appears beside the image; select a row, or click a vacuole, to see its marker measurements and any parasite count.

When the preview looks right, turn Live off and expand Actions if it is folded. Keep Save on and press Run. The console prints the output path when it finishes, and the results land in results/host_pathogen inside the first selected project.

The results build from small to large. vacuoles.csv has one row per vacuole: its host link, marker ratios, marker state and any parasite count. cells.csv rolls those up into host-cell infection and vacuole counts, and wells.csv summarises them per well.

Two more tables answer the biology. marker_states.csv shows joint marker states, and replication_distribution.csv the parasite counts per counted vacuole. Parasites without a usable parent link land in orphan_parasites.csv. Keep settings.json with them so your channel and threshold choices travel along.

One last check before comparing conditions: the denominators. Infection fractions use the measured host cells that were kept, so uninfected hosts count only if Measure retained them. Count distributions use only vacuoles with a known parasite count, and unknown never quietly becomes zero.
